newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Destruction of Bosnia homes on increase.
newsitem.headline: Destruction of Bosnia homes on increase.

text.p: Scores of homes have been blown up in northwestern Bosnia, dealing a blow to international efforts to reunite the war-torn country and help refugees return to their homes, the U.N. said on Friday.
"About 90 houses were destroyed in early morning hours on Thursday in several villages near Prijedor in Serb territory," Patrik Svensson, spokesman for the U.N. police forces said.
The U.N. said on Thursday that incidents began in the Sanski Most-Prijedor area earlier this week when people started using a U.N.-sponsored bus line aiming to bring Moslems and Serbs closer.
NATO reported destruction of 51 houses on Thursday by anti-tank mines in two former Moslem villages in Serb territory, southwest of Prijedor.

"Using mines to blow up shells of houses that refugees might fix up and move into is clearly designed to keep fear alive and to intimidate displaced people who may have wished to return to their former home," a NATO spokesman said.
Later on Thursday, 30 uninhabited houses in a former Serb village of Ljeskovica, southeast of Prijedor but on the Moslem- Croat side of the line, were gutted by fire, he said.
"It is intimidatory and it's aimed at returns and these are criminals that are doing it, whether they are organised at some high level or at a local level," NATO spokesman Major Simon Haselock said.
To demolish 51 houses in a comparatively short period of time requires good organisation, he said.
"There is no question that this was a substantive effort," Haselock said but could not say how many people did it or who organised them.
NATO recently introduced a tough-action plan to combat house destructions by increasing patrols in high-risk areas.

But their efforts were concentrated to the Sapna region in the northeast of the country in the Serb territory where some 70 explosions were reported in October and where Moslems are currently resettling in their former homes.
The leading humanitarian agency in charge of refugee returns was particularly alarmed by the development in the area.
The U.N. High Commissioner for Refguees was investing efforts to return refugees to their homes.
"This is clearly not a good sign for returns," Ariane Quentier of UNHCR said.
She said the UNHCR has been trying to organise a visit by Moslems to one of the villages in the area where explosions occured, which was 99 percent Moslem before the war but purely Serb now.
Haselock said that NATO's commander of ground forces, General Sir Michael Walker would travel to the region on Friday to discuss the situation with Serb, Moslem and NATO commanders on the ground.
